learn.title: How to Write Your First AI Eval - SallyAnn DeLucia, Arize AI
learn.headline: Hands-on workshop on writing pass/fail evals for an AI agent.
learn.reason: Evals are on your learning list; shows judge prompts and trace reading you can practise.

card.headline: A workshop shows how to write your first test for AI answers
card.gist: Someone from Arize AI teaches how to test AI answers properly. Clear pass or fail rules replace gut feeling.
card.picture: Think of a data quality check in an ETL job. You stop eyeballing a few rows and saying 'looks fine'. You write a rule, like 'no empty customer IDs', and run it on every row.
card.why_you: You are learning to test AI answers now. This shows the full path: read the step-by-step record, define good, then write the checks.
card.remember: Write down what a good answer means before testing anything.
card.term_meaning: Using one AI model to grade another model's answers against written pass or fail rules.
card.say_it: I read traces, write concrete pass/fail criteria, then build an LLM judge to apply them.
card.follow_up_why: Because eyeballing answers does not scale, so you need written pass or fail rules.
card.reality_check: A workshop by Arize AI's head of product, demonstrated in Arize's own tool.
card.try_it: Ask a local Ollama model five questions. Write one pass/fail rule and grade each answer.

learn.title: How to Build an AI Code Review Agent - Daksh Gupta, Greptile
learn.headline: How a code review agent gets better: cost, misses, and cheaper model routing.
learn.reason: Shows real agent cost and quality tradeoffs, a common interview topic you can retell.

card.headline: A code review company explains how to build your own review bot
card.gist: Greptile's co-founder explains how to build an AI that reviews code changes. A simple version misses bugs and nitpicks, so he lists fixes.
card.picture: Imagine hiring a new reviewer for your team's SQL. At first they miss bugs and complain about small style points. You give them past incident reports, project docs, and a second opinion from someone else.
card.why_you: It is a real example of improving an AI system one fix at a time. You can name these fixes in an interview.
card.remember: Simple review bots miss bugs. Past incidents and a different AI help.
card.term_meaning: Having a different AI model review the code, for example GPT reviewing code that Claude wrote.
card.say_it: For review agents, I'd use model inversion: GPT reviews Claude-written code, and vice versa.
card.follow_up_why: Because Greptile reports it catches about 10% more bugs.
card.reality_check: The numbers come from Greptile, a company that sells code review, not from independent tests.
card.try_it: Have Claude Code write a small function. Then ask a local Ollama model to review it.

learn.title: v0.40.11
learn.headline: Ollama adds small local classifier models that answer questions with probabilities.
learn.reason: The 2B to 27B models run free on your Mac and classify text with scores.

card.headline: Ollama can now speak aloud on Mac and adds yes-or-no models
card.gist: Ollama on Mac can now read text or a chat reply aloud. It also adds models that return a label or a yes or no.
card.picture: A chat model answers a question with a paragraph. These new models act more like an sklearn classifier. You get a label or yes/no, with a probability, not an essay.
card.why_you: You can try the speech feature on your Mac with Ollama. The labeling models come in four sizes, so check which fit your memory.
card.remember: Ask for a label, not an essay, when you need a decision.
card.term_meaning: A model that returns a label, a yes or no, or scored options with probabilities.
card.say_it: For tagging or routing, I'd use a decision model that returns a label with probabilities.
card.follow_up_why: Because the task only needs a label or yes/no, and these models are built to return that.
card.reality_check: From Ollama's own release notes; speech is stated for macOS only.
card.try_it: Update Ollama, then run: ollama run phonon "Hello from Ollama." and listen.
